findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled on return
findings.body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...), where ctx is the incoming request context. The apiserver cancels that parent as soon as the handler returns, which cancels the child immediately, so the 10s timeout never applies and the legacy write is aborted. Mode 3's safety copy to legacy therefore usually never lands, and the two stores diverge with no caller-visible error.

findings.title: Legacy create/update reuse the same object and UpdatedObjectInfo as storage
findings.body: Create passes the same obj pointer to Storage.Create and then to the async Legacy.Create. Unified storage mutates that object in place (UID, resourceVersion, timestamps). Legacy then persists those storage-assigned fields, or rejects the create because resourceVersion is already set. Update dropped the previous updateWrapper and passes the same rest.UpdatedObjectInfo into both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update. UpdatedObject is typically single-use (it consumes the patch or returns an already-applied object), so the second call fails or writes a different object than the one stored in unified storage. Either way the legacy copy is not a faithful safety write.

findings.title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy duration
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, the error path calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration. Update does the same on the storage-update error path (recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time). Operators will see storage outages as legacy latency/errors and will not see the storage failure in the storage series, so mode-3 rollout alerts and dashboards are wrong.

findings.title: Successful delete metric uses object name as the kind label
findings.body: On a successful Storage.Delete, recordStorageDuration is called with name (the object name) where every other path passes options.Kind. The kind label becomes unbounded cardinality (one series per deleted object) and no longer matches the kind label used by create/get/list, so the delete success metric cannot be aggregated with the rest of mode 3.

findings.title: Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage metric
findings.body: After the async Legacy.DeleteCollection returns, the code calls recordStorageDuration rather than recordLegacyDuration, using the legacy start time. Legacy delete-collection latency and errors are attributed to unified storage, and there is no legacy series for that method, so a failing safety delete of a collection is invisible on the legacy metrics.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are neither logged nor surfaced
findings.body: The goroutines that call Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection ignore the returned error except for a duration metric (and, for delete-collection, the wrong metric). There is no log line. Because the caller already returned success from unified storage, a failed safety write leaves legacy permanently behind with nothing in the logs to reconcile from.
